segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri and the peace chants reached prachodayat: may he stir, and the Gayatri read whole. Now Priya needs a chant for the stage. She's found one with a strange grammar.

English keeps a few words that only work for two: both, either, each other. Sanskrit goes further. Its verbs and pronouns have a whole set of forms for exactly two people, not one and not many. Grammarians call it the dual. And there's a peace chant written in it from start to finish. Which two? A teacher and a student, about to open a text together.
screen: `A GRAMMAR FOR EXACTLY TWO.` → `A TEACHER AND A STUDENT.`

segments.voice: The chant, from the Taittiriya Upanishad: saha navavatu, saha nau bhunaktu, saha viryam karavavahai, tejasvi navadhitam astu, ma vidvishavahai. Take it word by word. Saha: together. Navavatu is two words joined: nau, us two, and avatu, may it protect. May it protect us two together. Saha nau bhunaktu: may it nourish us two together. Saha viryam karavavahai: viryam is strength, and karavavahai, may we two do, may we two make. Listen to the ending, -vahai. That's the dual: a verb ending that counts exactly two. Tejasvi navadhitam astu: nau again, and adhitam, what has been studied. May our study, us two, be bright. And last, ma vidvishavahai: ma is don't, and vidvishavahai, the same two-person ending, may we two turn against each other. So: may we two not. Here's the puzzle's answer. The chant could have said we, the ordinary plural, the way the Gayatri does. It doesn't. Every verb counts two. Teacher and student say it together, and the grammar won't let either one stand outside it, above it, or alone. Even the last wish, not to fall out, needs both of them to keep it.
screen: `SAHA: TOGETHER.` · `NAU: US TWO.` · `-VAHAI: THE ENDING THAT COUNTS TWO.` · `MA VIDVISHAVAHAI: MAY WE TWO NOT.` · then, large: `EVERY VERB COUNTS TWO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you learn alongside, a teacher, a study partner, a friend who explains things. If your phone is near, send them one short line of thanks, then set it down. Sit for the rest of the time with the two of you in mind, side by side.
The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: saha navavatu, a peace chant in the dual, where every verb counts exactly two.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: karavavahai, may we two do; -vahai is a dual ending.

trapdoor: what you thought: the chant says we, like any group prayer.
what it means: every verb is in the dual: may it protect us two, may we two not turn against each other.
what a scholar hears: nau is the dual pronoun; karavāvahai and vidviṣāvahai are first person dual middle forms; the chant heads a section of the Taittiriya and is recited with the Katha.

chat.meaning: Saha navavatu uses the dual, the Sanskrit forms for exactly two: teacher and student, saying it together. Neither stands outside it.

notes: Peace chants, day 1 of 4 (1507–1510). Day 1769 (later this year) teaches saha navavatu by meaning (both, resentment in study); this day keeps to the dual grammar. Consider cross-reference when 1769 is next revised.

Grammar stated: nau as dual pronoun (nāv avatu by sandhi), avatu and bhunaktu as third singular imperatives ('may it'), karavāvahai and vidviṣāvahai as first person dual forms, adhītam 'what has been studied'. The subject 'it' is left unnamed (readers supply Brahman or 'he'). Confirm.
